title: Covertness as a resource constraint in quantum target sensing
authors: Yu Yang, Fengyu Guan, Shiping Guo, Ruifeng Liu, Pei Zhang, Fuli Li
abstract: Quantum covert target sensing aims to detect low-reflectivity targets embedded in the thermal environment while avoiding discovery by an adversary. This covertness requirement constrains the admissible probe energy, thereby imposing a trade-off between covertness and sensing performance. However, how this resource constraint determines the ultimate estimation precision of the target parameter remains largely unexplored. To fill this gap, we establish a unified framework connecting covert target discrimination with quantum-enhanced parameter estimation. We first present perturbative $ε$-covertness-induced bounds on the probe energy, which yield an admissible energy window narrowing as $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{ε/M})$. Moreover, we introduce the covertness-constrained quantum Fisher information (CCQFI) to quantify the ultimate precision of target-reflectivity estimation and assess its attainability with specific measurements. For Gaussian-distributed coherent-state (GCS) and two-mode squeezed vacuum (TMSV) probes, their CCQFIs scale as $\mathcal{O}(ε)$ and $\mathcal{O}(M)+\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{εM})+\mathcal{O}(ε)$, respectively. In particular, in the strong covertness regime $ε\to0$, the GCS CCQFI vanishes, whereas the TMSV retains a finite $\mathcal{O}(M)$ contribution exhibiting a pronounced metrological advantage. Besides, photon counting saturates the GCS CCQFI, whereas homodyne detection achieves a higher attainability for the TMSV probe. Our work identifies covertness as a quantitative resource constraint governing the metrological limits of quantum target sensing.
summary: This paper develops a theoretical framework connecting the requirement of remaining covert during quantum sensing with the ultimate achievable estimation precision. By introducing the covertness-constrained quantum Fisher information (CCQFI), the authors quantify how the need to evade detection limits the available probe energy. They show that different quantum states, like TMSV, can maintain superior metrological advantages even when severely constrained by the covertness requirement.
main_problem: The paper establishes a unified framework to quantify how the requirement of remaining covert (avoiding detection by an adversary) constrains the ultimate precision achievable in quantum target sensing.
main_result: The covertness constraint is identified as a quantitative resource that governs the metrological limits, showing that different quantum probes (GCS vs. TMSV) exhibit distinct scaling behaviors in the strong covertness regime.
method: The authors use quantum information theory tools, including the covertness-constrained quantum Fisher information (CCQFI), to bound the estimation precision for target reflectivity.
model_or_system: The system models quantum target sensing where a low-reflectivity target is probed. The analysis compares two Gaussian probes: Gaussian-distributed coherent-state (GCS) and Two-mode squeezed-vacuum (TMSV) states.
key_observables: Covertness-constrained Quantum Fisher Information (CCQFI) and Covertness-constrained Classical Fisher Information (CFI).
important_parameters: Covertness parameter ($\epsilon$), probe energy ($	ext{N}_s$), and the number of probe copies ($M$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on perturbative bounds for small $\epsilon$ and assumes the validity of Gaussian state descriptions for the probes.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the schematic setup of quantum covert target detection and show the numerical convergence of the CFI under different photon-number truncations.
paper_structure: The work progresses by first defining the covertness constraint via error bounds, then developing the CCQFI framework, and finally calculating and comparing the achievable precision limits for GCS and TMSV probes under this constraint.
why_interesting: This work directly bridges quantum estimation theory (metrology) with quantum security/detection theory (covertness), providing a resource-constrained view of quantum sensing that is highly relevant to quantum optics and quantum information.
